title: Resolves Come in the Measure of the Resolute
intro: Al-Mutanabbi wrote this for Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid prince of Aleppo, in 343 AH (954 CE), when the prince rebuilt the frontier fortress of al-Hadath, which its people had surrendered to the Byzantines in 337 AH and which the Byzantines had wrecked. While the walls were going up, the Byzantine commander Bardas Phokas came against it with an army of Byzantines, Armenians, Rus and Bulgars, and Sayf al-Dawla routed him and stayed until the building was finished; al-Ukbari and al-Barquqi say the poem was recited at al-Hadath on the day the prince laid the last battlement with his own hand. It opens with a maxim on great resolves and great men, then turns to the red fortress raised while spears clashed, the iron-clad enemy army of many tongues, the prince standing firm and the commander's flight, and ends with the poet's pride in his verse and a prayer for the prince. Al-Wahidi records that Sayf al-Dawla objected to the way lines 22 and 23 pair their halves, likening them to two lines of Imru' al-Qays that critics had faulted in the same way, and that the poet's defence of both won the prince over.

translation: Resolves come in the measure of the resolute,
and noble deeds come in the measure of the noble.
1.sharh: A man's undertakings are as large as he is: the bold attempt great things and the generous do great kindnesses. Al-Wahidi puts it as “men are the moulds of events”.

translation: In the eyes of the small, small things look great,
and in the eyes of the great, great things look small.
2.sharh: Small men are impressed by small deeds, and great men think little of great ones. The line points back to line 1 and forward to Sayf al-Dawla, for whom the feat at al-Hadath was nothing out of the ordinary.

translation: Sayf al-Dawla burdens his army with his own ambition,
a load that vast armies have failed to bear.
3.sharh: Sayf al-Dawla expects his soldiers to carry out every raid and campaign his ambition conceives, more than any army, however large, could manage. Al-Wahidi rejects a variant reading, “the vast seas”, as a mistake.

translation: He looks in other men for what he finds in himself,
and that is more than lions would claim.
4.sharh: He expects his men to be as brave as he is, though even lions would not pretend to such courage. The praise lies in the impossible demand: no one can match him, yet he asks it of everyone.

translation: The longest-lived of birds would give their lives for his weapons:
the vultures of the wilds, the young of them and the old.
5.sharh: Vultures, said to be the longest-lived of birds, young and old alike, would lay down their lives for Sayf al-Dawla's weapons, because his battles leave them more carrion than they could ever hunt.

translation: It would not harm them to be made without talons,
now that his swords and their hilts have been made.
6.sharh: Vultures could do without talons, since his swords do their hunting for them. The hilts stand for swords in hand; the same rhyme word returns in line 16 meaning horses' legs.

translation: Does al-Hadath the Red know its own colour?
Does it know which of its two waterers was the clouds?
7.sharh: Al-Hadath is so stained with Byzantine blood that it may not recognise its own colour, and it has been watered so freely by rain and by blood that it cannot tell which waterer was which. The next line names the second waterer.

translation: White clouds watered it before he came down on it;
when he drew near it, skulls watered it.
8.sharh: Before the prince arrived, the fortress was watered by rain from bright clouds; once he came and fought there, it was watered by blood from enemy skulls. These are the two waterers of line 7.

translation: He built it and raised it high while spear struck spear
and the waves of death crashed around it.
9.sharh: The prince built the fortress up while the battle raged around it, spear clashing with spear and death surging like a stormy sea. Building under fire is the heart of the poem's praise.

translation: There was something like madness upon it; now
the bodies of the slain hang on it as amulets.
10.sharh: The fortress had been like a madwoman, never at peace while the Byzantines kept attacking it. Now enemy corpses hang on its walls like amulets hung on the mad to cure them. Al-Ukbari says the poet first said “carrion” and took Sayf al-Dawla's “bodies” instead.

translation: Time's quarry, which it drove away: you brought it back
to the faith with your spears, and Time is humbled.
11.sharh: Time had hunted the fortress down like game and handed it to the Byzantines, who wrecked it. Sayf al-Dawla won it back for Islam with his spears and humbled Time, which had wanted otherwise.

translation: You make the nights forfeit all that you take,
and whatever they take from you, they must repay.
12.sharh: Whatever Sayf al-Dawla takes from the nights is lost to them for good, and whatever they take from him they have to pay back: he is stronger than Time. Al-Ukbari reports that the poet corrected a reader who made the nights the takers.

translation: When what you intend is an imperfect verb,
it is past before the jussives can be cast upon it.
13.sharh: A play on grammar: what the prince intends, an imperfect verb in the grammarians' terms, is already past, carried out, before any jussive particle can govern it, that is, before anyone can say “do not” or “let him”.

translation: How can the Byzantines and the Rus hope to tear it down
when these spear-thrusts are its foundations and its pillars?
14.sharh: The Byzantines and their Rus allies cannot hope to pull the fortress down: the spear-thrusts that drove them off now hold it up like foundations and pillars.

translation: They took it to judgement, and death was the judge:
the wronged did not die, and the wrongdoer did not live.
15.sharh: The Byzantines brought a case against the fortress, and death sat in judgement: the wronged party, the fortress, was allowed to live, and the wrongdoers were sentenced to die. The battle becomes a just trial.

translation: They came at you dragging iron, as if
they rode by night on steeds that had no legs.
16.sharh: The Byzantines came so heavily armoured that their horses' legs were hidden under trappings of mail, and the horses seemed to have none. Al-Ukbari notes that the rhyme word here means legs, so line 6, where it means hilts, is not repeated.

translation: When they flashed, the swords could not be told from them:
their clothes were of the swords' own kind, and their turbans.
17.sharh: In the sun the soldiers glittered like their own swords, since their clothes were mail and their headgear steel. Al-Ukbari laughs at a teacher who objected that Byzantines wore no turbans, missing that these turbans were made of steel.

translation: An army whose advance spans the earth, east and west,
and in the ear of Gemini its clamour rings.
18.sharh: The enemy army seemed to fill the earth from east to west as it advanced, and its din reached the stars. Al-Wahidi says the poet chose al-Jawza', Gemini, because the constellation was pictured in human form and so could have an ear.

translation: Every tongue and every nation gathered in it,
and only interpreters could make the talkers understood.
19.sharh: So many peoples and languages were mixed in the enemy army that its soldiers could only talk to one another through interpreters. Ibn al-Iflili lists Byzantines, Armenians, Rus, Bulgars and Slavs among them.

translation: What a time it was, whose fire melted the dross,
till nothing was left but a keen blade or a lion.
20.sharh: What an hour of battle that was: like a smith's furnace it melted away the dross, the weak men and poor weapons, and left only keen swords and lion-hearted men. The rhyme pairs sarim, “keen sword”, with dubarim, “lion”.

translation: Whatever could not cut through mail and spear-shaft shattered,
and those of the champions fled who could not stand the clash.
21.sharh: This is the dross of line 20: every sword too weak to cut through armour and spear-shafts broke, and every fighter who could not face the shock of battle ran. Al-Wahidi's text has “horsemen” for “champions”.

translation: You stood where no one standing doubted death,
as if you were in the eyelid of Destruction while it slept.
22.sharh: Sayf al-Dawla stood his ground where death seemed certain, as if shut inside Death's eyelid; but Death was asleep and did not see him. Al-Wahidi tells how the prince objected to the pairing of halves in this line and the next.

translation: Champions pass by you wounded and routed,
and your face is shining and your mouth smiling.
23.sharh: Wounded champions stream past in flight while the prince's face shines and he smiles at the danger. Answering the prince, the poet said he had paired death with its synonym in line 22 and set the routed men's frowns against his smile here.

translation: You went past the measure of courage and of wisdom
to the point where people say: you know the unseen.
24.sharh: His daring went so far beyond ordinary courage and judgement that people said he must know the future, since he fought like a man certain of victory. Ibn Jinni found courage an odd partner for knowledge of the unseen.

translation: You folded their two wings over the heart in a grip
under which the lesser feathers died, and the greater.
25.sharh: He drove the enemy's two flanks in on its centre and crushed the whole army. Having called the flanks wings, the poet makes their men feathers, the long flight feathers and the smaller ones beneath them, from the foremost to the hindmost.

translation: With blows that reached the heads while victory was away
and came down to the throats as victory arrived.
26.sharh: The swords struck the enemy's heads while victory was still absent and reached their throats as it arrived: so fast was the battle won. Ibn Jinni reads it as the prince counting no blow a victory until it splits a man to the chest.

translation: You scorned the Rudayni spears till you cast them aside,
till it seemed the sword was cursing the spear.
27.sharh: The prince despised the spear, which strikes from a distance, threw it away and fought hand to hand with the sword, the weapon of the truly brave, until the sword seemed to sneer at the spear for its cowardice.

translation: Whoever seeks a glorious conquest,
its keys are the white blades, light and keen.
28.sharh: Whoever wants a great victory must open it with swords. The Arabic for conquest, fath, means “opening”, and keys, mafatih, come from the same root, so the swords are literally the keys of conquest.

translation: You scattered them over the whole of al-Uhaydib
as silver coins are scattered over a bride.
29.sharh: He strewed the enemy dead all over the hill of al-Hadath as coins are showered on a bride at her wedding. Al-Ukbari counts the image among the poet's finest: a slaughter dressed as a celebration.

translation: The horses trample the nests on the peaks with you,
and food has grown plentiful around the nests.
30.sharh: His cavalry chased the fleeing Byzantines up to the mountain tops, trampling the nests of birds of prey, and the dead they left there made a feast round the nests.

translation: The eaglets think you have come to visit them
with their mothers, but they are hardy thoroughbreds.
31.sharh: When his horses reached the eagles' nests, the chicks mistook them for their mothers, so swift and lean were they; but they were tough thoroughbred chargers. Ibn al-Iflili reads it otherwise: the chicks thought he had brought their mothers, so much food did he leave them.

translation: When they slipped, you made them walk on their bellies,
as speckled snakes crawl over the ground.
32.sharh: Where the slopes were so steep that the horses lost their footing, he drove them on, crawling on their bellies like snakes. The line shows how hard the climb was and how relentless the pursuit.

translation: Is this Domestic to come on every day,
his nape blaming his face for coming on?
33.sharh: The Byzantine commander attacks day after day and runs away every time, so the back of his neck, which takes the blows in his flight, blames his face for leading it into the attack.

translation: Will he not know the lion's scent until he tastes it?
Even the beasts have learnt the scent of lions.
34.sharh: The commander will not believe in the lion until he has tasted its bite, though dumb beasts know the smell of lions and keep away. He keeps coming to fight Sayf al-Dawla and losing, which makes him more foolish than they are.

translation: They have robbed him of his son and his son-in-law's son,
and of his son-in-law: the prince's ruthless charges.
35.sharh: The prince's charges have already cost the commander his son, his son-in-law's son and his son-in-law, and still he comes back. Ibn al-Athir says his son Constantine was killed in an earlier raid, and that his son-in-law and grandson were captured at al-Hadath.

translation: He fled, thanking his comrades that he escaped the blades,
because their heads and wrists kept the blades busy.
36.sharh: The commander got away grateful to his men, whose heads and wrists kept the swords busy while he fled. Their deaths bought his escape.

translation: He understands the voice of the Mashrafi swords among them,
though the voices of swords are foreign tongues.
37.sharh: The clash of swords speaks no language, yet the commander understood it perfectly: it told him his men were being cut down and he had better run. Al-Wahidi says he understood by inference, not by hearing.

translation: He is glad of what he gave you, and not from ignorance:
a plundered man who escapes you is the winner.
38.sharh: The commander is glad of all he left behind, not because he misjudges his loss but because anyone who escapes Sayf al-Dawla alive has won. Al-Ukbari cites the proverb “safety is one of the two spoils”.

translation: You are not a king who routed his equal:
you are the Oneness of God, routing polytheism.
39.sharh: His victory was not one king beating another of his rank; it was Islam's faith in one God routing those who worship more than one. The commander, in this view, was no match for him.

translation: All Adnan is honoured by him, not Rabi'a alone,
and the world takes pride in him, not the Awasim alone.
40.sharh: All the Arabs descended from Adnan share the honour of his deeds, not just his own tribe of Rabi'a, and the whole world boasts of him, not only the frontier lands he rules. Al-Ukbari would have preferred “you” to “him” here.

translation: Yours is the praise for the pearls whose wording is mine,
for you are the one who gives them, and I string them.
41.sharh: The pearls of the poem are the prince's deeds; the poet only threads them on a string, so the credit is the prince's. Arabic uses one verb, nazama, for stringing pearls and for composing verse.

translation: Your gifts gallop with me into battle,
so I am not blamed, and you have nothing to regret.
42.sharh: He rides into battle on the horses the prince gave him. He cannot be blamed for taking them, since he repays them with gratitude and praise, and the prince has no reason to regret giving them.

translation: On every steed that flies to it on its legs
when the din of fighting falls upon its ears.
43.sharh: The gifts of line 42 are horses that fly into battle on their legs the moment they hear the confused shouting of the fighters. The line finishes the sentence begun in the one before.

translation: O you sword that is never sheathed,
that no one doubts, and that nothing shields from.
44.sharh: He addresses the prince by his title, “the Sword of the State”, as a sword that is never sheathed, whose edge no one doubts and against which nothing gives protection. Al-Wahidi and al-Ukbari have the line in the second person.

translation: Joy to the striking of heads, to glory and to high rank,
to those who hope in you, and to Islam: you are safe.
45.sharh: He congratulates everything the prince sustains on his safe return from battle: the striking of enemy heads, glory, high rank, everyone who hopes for his bounty, and Islam itself, since each of them depends on him.

translation: Why should the Merciful not guard your two edges for ever,
when through you He is always splitting His enemies' heads?
46.sharh: God will surely guard both edges of this sword for as long as He guards anything, since He is forever splitting His enemies' heads with it. The poem ends on a pun on the prince's title: he is God's own sword.

1.1.6.head: العَزيمَة
1.1.6.meaning: Resolves: what a man has firmly decided to do; the plural of azima.

3.1.2-3.meaning: Sayf al-Dawla, “Sword of the State”: the title of Ali ibn Abdallah ibn Hamdan (303–356 AH, 915–967 CE), prince of Aleppo and al-Mutanabbi's patron.

3.2.5.head: الخِضرِم
3.2.5.meaning: Vast, numerous; khidrim is anything large and abundant.

5.1.1.head: فَدّى
5.1.1.meaning: Says “may I be your ransom”: offers its life for another.

6.2.4.head: القائِم
6.2.4.meaning: Hilts; qa'im is the grip of a sword.

7.1.2.meaning: Al-Hadath: a fortress on the Byzantine frontier between Malatya, Sumaysat and Mar'ash, on a hill called al-Uhaydib. Its people surrendered it to the Byzantines in 337 AH; Sayf al-Dawla rebuilt it in 343 AH (954 CE).

7.1.3.meaning: “The Red”: red with Byzantine blood, says al-Wahidi; al-Ukbari also mentions red stone, and Yaqut says the fortress was called the Red for its red soil.

10.2.5.head: تَميمَة
10.2.5.meaning: Amulets, hung on a person against madness and the evil eye.

11.1.1.meaning: Quarry: game that is hunted and driven off.

11.2.3.head: الخَطِّيّ
11.2.3.meaning: Khatti: spears, named after al-Khatt, a port in Bahrain.

11.2.5.meaning: Humbled; literally with its nose in the dust.

13.1.6.meaning: Imperfect: in grammar, the verb form for what is not yet done.

13.2.6.head: الجازِم
13.2.6.meaning: Jussives: in grammar, the particles that put a verb in the jussive, such as lam, “did not”, and la, “do not”.

14.1.4.head: الرّوس
14.1.4.meaning: The Rus: a northern people who fought in the Byzantine army; al-Dhahabi says the commander gathered Turks, Rus, Bulgars and Khazars for this battle.

17.1.5.meaning: “The white ones”: swords, for their gleam.

18.1.1.meaning: Khamis: a great army, said to be named for its five divisions.

18.2.3.head: الجَوزاء
18.2.3.meaning: Al-Jawza': Gemini, a constellation pictured in human form.

20.1.4.meaning: Dross: the base metal mixed into silver or gold; here weak men and poor weapons.

20.2.6.meaning: A powerful lion; a fearless warrior.

25.1.2.head: جَناح
25.1.2.meaning: The two wings of an army: its right and left flanks.

27.1.2.head: الرُّدَينِيّ
27.1.2.meaning: Rudayni: spears named after Rudayna, a woman of al-Yamama who made spears with her husband.

29.1.3.meaning: Al-Uhaydib, “the little humpback”: the hill on which al-Hadath stands.

29.2.4.meaning: A bride; coins were showered on her at the wedding.

30.1.4.head: الوَكر
30.1.4.meaning: Nests of birds of prey, eyries.

33.1.5.meaning: Dumustuq: the Domestic, commander of the Byzantine armies, from the Greek domestikos; here Bardas Phokas.

33.2.1.head: قَفا
33.2.1.meaning: The nape, the back of the neck.

37.1.3.head: المَشرَفِيّ
37.1.3.meaning: Mashrafi: swords named after al-Masharif, villages on the edge of Arabia.

39.2.2.meaning: Tawhid: faith in the oneness of God; here Islam.

40.1.2.meaning: Adnan: the forefather of the northern Arabs, Rabi'a and Mudar among them.

40.1.5.meaning: Rabi'a: Sayf al-Dawla's own tribal group, through Taghlib.

40.2.5.meaning: Al-Awasim: the fortified borderlands of northern Syria, ruled from Aleppo.

41.2.4.meaning: One who strings pearls; also one who composes verse.

46.1.5.head: حَدّ
46.1.5.meaning: The two edges of a sword.
